column3: It repeats the reciprocal bringing forth of living from dead and dead from living, while grounding it in the splitting of seed and kernel.
Life, death, and return to God state the governing sequence that the focus concludes with resurrection.
It joins life and death in the earth with emergence from it, closely matching the focus's final human extraction.
The same reciprocal life-from-death formula is set beside the alternation of night and day, reinforcing divinely ordered transformation.
Its before-and-after reversal under God's command supports the surah's wider pattern of conditions changing in appointed time.
It explicitly asks whether the Creator has power to give life to the dead, making the focus's resurrection conclusion direct.
It states that God revives the earth after its death, the focus's immediate natural sign, though without its human conclusion.
Creation begins and is then repeated before the return to God, directly supplying the resurrection framework of the passage.
The objection to being brought out alive after death directly frames the conclusion affirmed by the focus.
Revived dead land is explicitly identified with resurrection, giving the rain-and-earth image its stated eschatological force.
Rain revives dead earth as a sign, a close natural parallel already established more fully by the earlier cards.
It voices the denial that people reduced to dust and bones can be brought out, directly opposing the focus's final claim.
The reciprocal bringing forth of life and death is coupled with divine governance, closely paralleling the focus's wording and claim.
Divine help in the local victory passage contributes only the surrounding surah theme of God's effective action.
It presents rain reviving dead earth as an acknowledged divine act, supporting the focus's observable premise.
Its ordered signs include rain reviving earth after death, broadening the focus's natural process without adding resurrection language.
Universal obedience to God supplies a broad sovereignty frame but no specific life-from-death transition.
Succession in the land after former peoples offers a distant pattern of replacement rather than bodily revival.
Measured rain revives a dead land and explicitly concludes, "thus you will be brought forth," closely matching both halves of the focus.
The accusation against Musa has no useful connection to the focus's life, death, earth, or resurrection sequence.
Waiting for someone to come out is a different use of emergence and adds little to resurrection.
The showing of God's dominion to Abraham gives a general certainty frame but no specific revival insight.
The named term and denial of meeting God establish the passage's resurrection horizon without restating its natural sign.
Water makes humbled earth stir and swell, then explicitly proves the giver of its life can revive the dead.
The exposure of hidden rancor uses bringing-out language in a distinct moral setting.
The despair of criminals when the Hour rises immediately continues the focus's resurrection declaration.
God's causing death and life directly affirms the paired dominion, though it lacks the focus's extraction and earth image.
Divine knowledge of what enters and exits earth provides only a broad movement pattern around the focus's emergence.
Humans are created from earth, returned to it, and brought forth again, a near-exact structural parallel to the focus.
Rain producing diverse plants supplies the productive-earth background, but not the earth's death or human resurrection.
A single call brings people out of the earth, directly elucidating the focus's concluding future passive emergence.
The fate of stronger prior peoples offers the local warning context for denying the appointed meeting with God.
Its question about belief after God's signs only generally supports the evidential role of the natural signs.
Its catalogue includes rain reviving earth after death, but the broader sign-list adds less than direct resurrection parallels.
Separation on the Day the Hour rises develops the consequences of the resurrection announced in the focus.
God gives life and death and remains heir, affirming divine dominion over the life cycle without emergence language.
A bodily fluid's emergence is a distinct physical origin image, only loosely related to the focus's bringing forth.
The catalogue of believing men and women does not clarify the focus's life-death-resurrection sequence.
The speakers recall two deaths and two lives and seek a way out, illuminating the existential stakes of life and emergence.
The divine names Living and Self-Subsisting provide a theological ground for the focus's life-giving action.
Rome's defeat supplies only the local surah setting for reversal, not the focus's stated transformation.
The brothers' plan to kill or cast out Yusuf does not add to the focus's resurrection meaning.
Pearls and coral emerging from the seas share only the general image of something coming forth.
Defeat followed by victory develops the surah's reversal pattern, but remains distinct from reviving the dead.
Dedicating life and death to God reinforces their divine ownership, though not their transformation or return.
Deliverance from distress offers a broad rescue analogy but no life-from-death or earth-revival detail.
Its contrast between persons and deeds is not a specific contribution to the focus's natural-resurrection argument.
The question about believing after this discourse adds no distinct insight beyond a general call to accept signs.
The Living, Self-Subsisting God's unfailing preservation supports the divine capacity behind life and resurrection.
God's unbroken promise reinforces the certainty of the surah's announced future outcomes, including its resurrection claims.
It directly gives the sequence of life, death, and renewed life, closely supporting the focus's final resurrection claim.
The detailed exposition of signs and possible return provides only a general rhetorical parallel.
Creation, provision, death, and life are assigned exclusively to God, directly expanding the focus's life-and-death agency.
Solomon's request for a unique kingdom has no material connection to the focus.
Banning expulsion from homes uses a different social sense of bringing out.
Return to Hell is a distinct final destination and does not illuminate earthly revival or resurrection.
The earth holding the living and dead offers a loose spatial backdrop for the focus's earth-and-life contrast.
Clear revealed signs and guidance do not specifically develop the focus's natural sign.
The command to glorify God at morning and evening is adjacent context but adds no life-death relation.
Repentance after punishment is a temporal reversal with little specific connection to bodily restoration.
Yusuf's establishment in the land is a social reversal, not a life-from-death parallel.
The inability to make the blind hear gives the passage's metaphorical death context, contrasting with God's actual life-giving power.
Rain after despair and the spread of mercy faintly echoes restoration, but not earth's death or resurrection.
Dead earth is revived and yields grain; the tangible production from it strongly develops the focus's earth-revival sign.
The denial that death and dust can lead to return directly contests the focus's announced human emergence.
A people are made to die and then given life, an enacted reversal that supports divine power despite its distinct narrative setting.
It explicitly points to God reviving earth after death and identifies Him as the reviver of the dead, directly restating the focus's proof.
Praise across heaven and earth at appointed times is adjacent liturgical context without a specific revival link.
Being brought forth for humankind is a communal vocation, not emergence from death.
Universal submission and return to God provide a broad eschatological frame but no life-death mechanism.
Revived dead land is explicitly likened to coming forth, making the focus's earth image a direct resurrection analogy.
The contrast of truth and error provides a general theological boundary, not a new resurrection connection.
Rain revives earth after death within the same surah's signs, closely supporting the focus, though less explicit than 30:50.
The disconnected opening letters add no interpretable relation to the focus.
The question whether dust and bones will be resurrected directly states the objection answered by the focus.
The bringing forth of pasture offers a limited natural emergence image without death or human resurrection.
Following desire without knowledge relates only indirectly to the passage's contrast between hearing and spiritual blindness.
The demonstration of how God gives life to the dead provides a concrete resurrection proof, though not the focus's earth analogy.
Cosmic rupture over an attribution to God has no useful link to the focus's life-death sequence.
The release of rain from clouds establishes the preceding stage of the surah's earth-revival sequence.
Abraham's confession that God causes death and then life directly supports the paired divine action in the focus.
God's dominion over heavens and earth includes giving life and death, a broad authority parallel.
The rejection of signs in the Quran belongs to the surah's polemical setting but adds no particular revival insight.
God's universal kingship includes giving life and death, linking that dominion to the call to faith.
Restoring the earth after its repair is an environmental contrast, only distantly related to reviving dead land.
The metaphor of the dead who cannot hear follows the focus and sharpens the contrast between physical and moral lifelessness.
Division after clear evidence has no particular connection beyond the broad theme of rejecting signs.
Breaking covenants and corrupting earth are morally contrary to repair, but do not explain life after death.
Sleep, work, and divine bounty form another local sign, only loosely connected to recurring life rhythms.
The instruction not to die except in submission concerns faithful ending, not resurrection or revivification.
The Book's revelation from the Mighty, Wise gives no specific addition to the focus.
Water bringing forth grain and vegetation offers a concise productive-earth parallel, without the focus's death-and-resurrection claim.
The small number among later people has no connection to the focus.
Inherited association and responsibility are unrelated to emergence from death beyond a temporal term.
A tunnel in earth or ladder to heaven is a different movement image and does not clarify resurrection.
Forcing the Prophet out of the land is a political expulsion, distinct from being brought out after death.
Relief after adversity is a general reversal and does not add to the focus's natural or eschatological sequence.
Expulsion from the Garden is a different, punitive use of bringing out.
The shade of black smoke does not contribute to the focus.
Iblis's commanded expulsion is a distinct judgmental use of coming out with no resurrection insight.
It gives the full human sequence from lifelessness to life, death, renewed life, and return to God.
God gives life to the dead as a sign for understanding, furnishing an enacted proof of resurrection.
The restoration of a dead town and the witness's revival make divine re-creation concrete.
Giving life to the dead by God's permission supplies a prophetic sign of the life-giving power at issue.
The same raising of the dead by God's permission reinforces that life restored remains divine action.
Creation from earth, an appointed death, and a final term provide a compact human life-cycle frame.
It states that God will resurrect the dead and that all will return to Him.
Nightly death and daytime raising offer a recurring experiential analogy for life after death.
The movement from death to life supplies a moral counterpart to the focus's physical transformation.
Rain revives earth after its death and the verse explicitly compares that process to bringing out the dead.
God originates creation and then repeats it before the universal return, directly supporting resurrection.
The challenge asks who originates creation and then repeats it, isolating the focus's central divine act.
It voices amazement at becoming dust and then entering a new creation, a direct denial of resurrection.
It explicitly affirms God's true promise to resurrect those who die.
Creation, death, and return to weakness establish that human life remains under God's changing control.
The objection about bones and fragments becoming a new creation directly contests the focus's conclusion.
The reply that God can restore even stone or iron broadens the focus's claim beyond ordinary decay.
The divine call brings people forth to answer, directly paralleling emergence at resurrection.
Being reduced to bones and dust yet raised in a new creation restates the disputed future emergence.
The leveling of the earth and gathering of all people supplies the assembled outcome of resurrection.
Life, death, and being raised alive are joined in a concise prophetic formula.
It explicitly names birth, death, and being raised alive, closely framing the focus's final transition.
The making of every living thing from water supplies a complementary natural origin sign.
The folding of heaven is paired with repeating creation as it first began, an explicit re-creation analogy.
Human formation and earth revived by rain culminate in a detailed proof for resurrection.
It states that God gives life to the dead and is capable of everything.
The certainty of the Hour is joined to God raising all who are in graves.
Human death is stated as an unavoidable stage before the following resurrection declaration.
It explicitly says that people will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection.
God gives life and causes death while alternating night and day, extending the focus's ordered transformations.
Originating creation and then repeating it is explicitly posed as a divine act.
It directs attention to how God begins creation and then repeats it, making observation a proof of return.
The command to observe creation on earth leads directly to God's production of the final creation.
Repeating creation is declared easy for God, directly reinforcing the focus's promised extraction.
Creating and resurrecting humanity is compared to creating and resurrecting a single soul.
Death is followed by return to God, supplying the immediate individual transition implied by the focus.
Water brought to barren land and producing crops gives the agricultural precursor to the focus's revived-earth sign.
The objection that scattered fragments will become a new creation directly opposes resurrection.
God gives life to the dead and records what they have sent ahead, coupling resurrection with accountability.
The trumpet blast brings people forth from graves toward their Lord.
Human origin from a drop confronts the denier's claim, preparing the argument for re-creation.
The question of who revives decayed bones directly states the resurrection objection.
The One who originated bones the first time is identified as able to revive them.
The question whether dust and bones will be raised repeats the focus's eschatological challenge.
The inclusion of former ancestors intensifies the claim of universal restoration after death.
It frames death and dust as the condition from which judgment is nevertheless expected.
The taking and releasing of souls in death and sleep gives a recurrent analogy for divine control of life.
After the trumpet's deathly blast, another blast raises all to standing and looking on.
The greater creation of heavens and earth supplies an argument from divine creative capacity for human re-creation.
God gives life and causes death, then brings a decreed matter into being by command.
God's exclusive guardianship is defined by giving life to the dead and unlimited power.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers all for the Day of Resurrection.
The Creator of heavens and earth is explicitly declared able to give life to the dead.
Blessed rain produces gardens and grain from above, supplying the process behind the ensuing resurrection analogy.
The denial of a new creation is answered by recalling the first creation.
God alone gives life and death, and the final journey returns to Him.
The earth splits open and people emerge swiftly; the gathering is declared easy for God.
The question whether dust and bones will be resurrected repeats the central objection.
The reminder that God created humankind provides the premise for His ability to recreate them.
Knowledge of the first creation is presented as a basis for remembering the possibility of re-creation.
Divine dominion over life and death is set within universal sovereignty.
The denial of being raised is answered with an oath that people will be raised and informed of their deeds.
People emerge rapidly from graves, depicting the focus's final bringing forth.
Human growth from the earth supplies an earth-based origin parallel to the focus's earth-based emergence.
God returns people to the earth and will bring them forth from it again.
The question whether bones will be gathered directly states the resurrection dispute.
God's ability to restore even fingertips makes the promised reconstruction exact and individual.
The trumpet's sounding brings people forth in groups.
The question about return after death introduces the coming emergence.
One overwhelming cry initiates the resurrection event.
After that cry, people are suddenly on the open plain.
Death and burial are named as the stage preceding God's later raising.
God will raise the human being when He wills.
Graves are overturned, directly depicting the release of their dead.
The earth's stretching prepares the paired scene of its contents being expelled.
The earth casts out what is within it, a direct terrestrial image of emergence.
The earth's emptying occurs in obedience to its Lord, identifying the command behind the release.
God's power to return the human being supports re-creation, though the precise return remains open.
The earth's final convulsion introduces the last disclosure of what it contains.
The earth brings out its burdens, a direct image of contents emerging from it.
All creatures are ultimately gathered to their Lord, extending the focus's return beyond human emergence.
Returning as God first originated people provides a concise creation-and-return frame.
The divine call to what gives life supplies a moral counterpart to the focus's life-giving action.
The Creator can remove people and bring a new creation, reinforcing that existence is not beyond replacement.
The changed earth and heavens on the final day provide the cosmic setting for resurrection and return.
The sleepers' discovery is used to establish that God's promise and the Hour are true.
At death, the wrongdoer asks to be sent back, exposing the irreversibility of ordinary earthly life.
The barrier until the day people are raised distinguishes death from the final resurrection.
The question of whether people were created purposelessly culminates in their return to God.
The false gods' inability to control death, life, or resurrection contrasts with the power named in the focus.
The plea to be returned after seeing the truth portrays the accountability that follows resurrection.
The distinction between living and dead supports the passage's wider physical and moral life-death contrast.
God apportions death and can replace people and produce them in an unknown form.
The One who spread humanity across the earth will gather them back to Himself.
The Lord of east and west is sworn able to replace people with better others.
